notes.line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4
notes.teaches: The way to take a freeing pawn break off the board is to cover its landing square with a pawn of your own — a second pawn on the fourth rank looks like a slow space-grab and is really prophylaxis: the break the defender's whole setup is built around simply stops existing.
notes.explains: The pawn comes to c4 and covers b5 and d5. The central break to d5 is the move this defence uses to free itself, and it is now met by a pawn rather than a piece. Nothing is attacked; the position becomes one where the defender has space to hold and no lever to open it with.

notes.line: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 c4 Nf6 Nc3 Nxd4 Qxd4
notes.teaches: Trading knights in a clamped position helps the side with less space, so recapture with the piece that makes the trade cost something — a queen that lands hitting a knight and two pawns at once means the simplification the defender wanted has handed over three tempi instead.
notes.explains: The knights have come off in the centre and the queen takes back. From d4 she hits the knight on f6 and the pawns on a7 and d7, while holding the pawns of the clamp behind her. The exchange that was supposed to relieve the cramped side has instead put the queen on the strongest square on the board.
